items.title: Fostering Resilience in Adolescents at Risk: Study protocol for a cluster randomized controlled trial within the resilience school-based intervention

items.summary: Introduction: Basic life support training in school age is a topical issue because, with adequate training, any person can help save a life.Methods: Cluster clinical trial with data collection through an ad hoc self-administered, semi -structured questionnaire. The target population encompassed the students aged 4--6 years enrolled in 49 educational centres. The centres were randomly allocated to the intervention or control group. The intervention group was trained with the RCParvulari (R) methodology, consisting of theoretical and practical training on the first link of the chain of survival. The control group only received theoretical training. We evaluated participants before and immediately after the intervention and between 3 and 12 months post-intervention by means of the ques-tionnaire. We assessed the acquisition and retention over time of the knowledge and skills covered in the training compared to previous trainings in both groups.Results: A total of 1327 schoolchildren (79% of the target population) participated. The level of knowledge acquired immediately after training and after 3-12 months compared to baseline was significantly better (P <.001) in the intervention group than in the control group, both in early recognition and contacting of emergency services (112) and in remembering the "mouth -nose-eyes " mnemonic.Conclusions: The RCParvulari (R) methodology significantly contributed to an improved ability to recognize a possible medical emergency, start the chain of survival by alerting an adult and call the 112 emergency number in students in the last year of preschool education.
items.title: RCParvulari training: A basic life support training methodology applied to 5-year-old students: Effectiveness in a cluster-randomized clinical trail

items.summary: Offline reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on a fixed pool of sampled responses and typically supervises every token of every response, although responses and tokens are not equally informative. We study which ones to supervise through the Gibbs-optimal policy of KL-regularized RLVR, which offline training targets, and measure the mismatch between a policy and this target with a bidirectional KL divergence. At the reference policy, this mismatch factorizes exactly and separates the two outcomes: correct responses contribute mainly through the forward term, concentrated on their low-probability tokens, and incorrect responses through the reverse term, concentrated on the responses the policy generates often and on their high-probability tokens. Based on this analysis, we propose GIST (Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection), a two-level selection method that approximates these principles with signals available before training. GIST uses the sampling temperature to select correct responses on-policy and incorrect responses near the policy's mode, and it uses the initial policy's token probabilities to supervise only the tokens where the mismatch lies. Applied to two offline training objectives, GIST raises the average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH-500, and MBPP for all three models under both objectives. In a controlled comparison on Qwen3-0.6B/GSM8K, it outperforms seven selection baselines that choose from the same candidates while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates of the same prompts.
items.title: GIST: Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection for Offline RLVR

items.summary: This deposit contains the data and the analysis code that reproduce the Methods and Results of a systematic review of polymer-based dental materials incorporating an engineered self-healing mechanism. The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework on 26 October 2026 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QCZFY) before formal screening and before any data were extracted. The review separates three contrasts that the literature conflates under the single heading of healing efficiency: C-I, the baseline penalty of the self-healing material in its virgin state against a capsule-free control; C-II, the recovery of the repaired material against the same material in its virgin state; and C-III, the net position of the repaired material against a conventional material without a healing system. The effect measure is the log ratio of means, back-transformed to a ratio and a percentage. Contents. The extraction matrix holds 105 arm-level rows covering four studies and 17 harmonised outcomes, each row linked to the exact formulation of both arms, the source page and the provenance of the value. Four further tables record the full-text eligibility decisions for the 48 assessed reports, the re-screening of the 96 discarded reports against the registered criteria, the characteristics of the studies carrying extracted data, and the register of 16 departures from the registered protocol. The R pipeline recomputes the 89 arm-level contrasts, the three pre-specified contrasts, the efficient-frontier criterion, both manuscript figures and the main and supplementary effect tables. A validation script asserts 21 reported values and halts the pipeline on any mismatch. Reproduction. R 4.4 or later with the metafor package is the only requirement. Running "Rscript run_all.R" from the root of the package regenerates every output in a few seconds and writes a session record alongside them. Limits of these data. Sixty of the 105 rows derive wholly or partly from provisional single-reader readings of figure panels and were not validated by duplicate digitisation; the provenance columns identify them. Five contrasts have a mean of zero in the numerator or the denominator, so the ratio of means is undefined for them. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were not assessed. Arm-level data were extracted from four of the 39 included studies. Licensing. Data and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; the code under R/, run_all.R and legacy/ is released under the MIT Licence.
items.title: Self-healing dental polymers: extraction matrix and analysis code for a systematic review with endpoint harmonisation

items.summary: PREPRINT SUBMITTED TO RENEW 2026 CONFERENCE.   MoodyMarine is an open-access weakly nonlinear potential flow solver for wave-body and mooring interactions. In this study the capabilities of MoodyMarine for modeling tension-leg-platform (TLP) type floating offshore wind turbines (FOWT) is assessed. A TLP-type platform has been simulated for four wave cases of increase wave steepness and compared to experimental data measurements of surge, heave, pitch, and mooring-line tension. A qualitatively and quantitatively comparison has been carried out using the root-mean-square error (RMSE), the relative root-mean-square-error (RRMSE), and the correlation coefficient (R). A numerical calibration was carried out for the baseline wave condition showing that the required initial experimental mooring stiffness had to be reduced from K = 132N/mm to K = 50N/mm to ensure good agreement between experimental and numerical data. Pitch motion agreement improved significantly (88.4 % reduction in RRMSE), while surge responses experienced small variations since surge is dominated by wave excitation rather than tendon stiffness. Mooring line tensions showed only a small improvement, as the baseline tension errors were already low. For the rest of the validation cases MoodyMarine showed good agreement with the experimental data while keeping the computational time to 0.152 s of CPU time per 1 s of simulated time.
items.title: NUMERICAL VALIDATION OF A FLOATING OFFSHORE WIND TLP-TYPE PLATFORM USING MOODYMARINE

items.summary: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.
items.title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors

items.summary: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
items.title: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models

items.summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
items.title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

items.summary: Code, data and outputs that reproduce a study of carbon embodied in China–EU trade and of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The archive covers three analyses: (1) CO2 embodied in China–EU27 trade, 2011–2022, from a global multi-regional input–output model (EXIOBASE 3.9.6, with release 3.8.2 for reconciliation and sensitivity); (2) China's potential CBAM certificate costs, 2026–2034; (3) EU27 imports from higher- and lower-carbon origins after CBAM reporting began, using a PPML triple-difference design on monthly Eurostat Comext data, January 2018 to July 2026. It contains the Python, R and Stata code, the analysis panel, derived input–output results, CBAM parameter files, codebooks, download manifests with checksums, and the output tables, figures and logs. The EXIOBASE 3.9.6 carbon multipliers and the ICAP daily price data are not included, in line with the source licences; the code to rebuild or process them is provided. Start with README_replication_archive.md. Code is released under the MIT licence and data under CC BY-SA 4.0 or CC BY 4.0, as set out in LICENSE.md.
items.title: Replication archive: Embodied CO2 in China–EU trade and early responses to the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism

items.summary: This deposit contains Stata replication code, execution instructions, and aggregate reference outputs for a study of public old-age pensions and private household transfers in Mexico, with comparative evidence from Chile. The analysis uses ENIGH 2008–2024 and CASEN survey microdata, which must be obtained from their original providers. The code reproduces the main empirical results and selected supplementary analyses. Additional Python-only analyses are not included. No individual- or household-level data are redistributed.
items.title: Replication code for public old-age pensions and private household transfers

items.summary: Study-Specific Replication Instructions for Study 1 from Nancekivell, Shah, & Gelman (2020): “Maybe they’re born with it, or maybe it’s experience: Toward a deeper understanding of the learning style myth.” Journal of Educational Psychology, 112 (2), 221-235. DOI of original article: https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/edu0000366 Briefly, the steps you take to complete a CREP replication of this project are: Sign up , and wait to get your project number and related information. Follow Part I of the Step-by-Step Guide to prepare your project's Replication Recipe Pre-Registration file (see template here ). Request a review when your project is prepared; revise as necessary. Once approved by your local IRB, collect, analyze, and write up your data, including a completed data template (found within the files on this page; "CREP_nancekivell_data_template.xlsx") Follow Part II of your Step-by-Step Guide (includes creating a new version of your project and uploading your Replication Recipe Post-Completion  file [template here] ) Request another review when your completion files are posted; revise as necessary. Link both registrations in "Related Works" of your Zenodo project. Request a badge ; the CREP team will upload one to the top of your Zenodo project to indicate that you have completed the project lifecycle.   Replication Guidelines Original Materials to Use for Your Replication The original materials for the study can be found within "files."  Sample Size and Extensions Per CREP rules, collect the same N as the original; if the original N > 100, 100 participants is sufficient.  CREP can be flexible on N if participants are difficult to obtain at your institution. If your team runs a  Direct+ replication with additional survey items or within-participants conditions (e.g., running an additional set of statements), place added items  at the very end , after the seriousness check, so they cannot affect the exposure or truth-judgment phases.  If your team runs a Direct+ replication with additional between-participants conditions (e.g., an entirely different set of statements for one group), plan on running additional participants (100 for the direct replication and 100 more for each between-participants condition). Notes from the author No additional information was provided by the author.
items.title: CREP Replication of Study 1 from Nancekivell, Shah, & Gelman (2020)

items.summary: This record holds the output of the benchmark harness that compares WormIE's over-representation, ranked-list enrichment, per-sample gene set scoring and DESeq2 runs with native R/Bioconductor, with timings. It also holds the comparison of WormIE's Gene Ontology over-representation with clusterProfiler. report.md and report-go.md are the two reports cited in the WormIE manuscript. benchmark-results.zip holds the full result tree, including the per-run data files behind both reports. benchmark-sessioninfo-R.txt lists the R version and packages of the native arm. The timings were measured on an Apple M2 with 24 GB of memory, with 10 repeats for each arm. The harness is in the benchmark folder of the application repository at https://github.com/sherlynpw/wormie (MIT license).
items.title: WormIE benchmark results: agreement with native R/Bioconductor

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.
items.title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application

items.summary: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.
items.title: Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement
